doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: The overlooked 1970s generation
summary: Kirchner says his generation and the 1970s jazz scene are being overlooked and erased, which angers him as a historian.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: So lastly, this is sort of an odd question but musically or politically or in any regard, is there something that could come up in a conversation that would really get, I guess the phrase is get your dander up? That would make you respond emphatically and be angry?

Well in part I feel like my generation has been kind of overlooked, the generation that came up in the 70s. You know I won’t go into naming names but I think you understand what I’m talking about. You know I feel like there was a whole generation of people who came up when I did in the 70s and our contributions have largely been overlooked. You know and we didn’t get a lot of the opportunities we should have. So that, you know, when, or for example I told you earlier about all the stuff I heard in New York in the 70s, in the early 70s you know and often you hear it written and said by various people who don’t know, who weren’t there, who say that oh there was nothing happening in jazz in the 70s, you know it was this period of doldrums. And that is total crap. I mean I mentioned all the things that I heard in New York in the 70s and that was a fraction of what was going on. There was so much happening at that point, but you had to be there to know about it, and all these people who weren’t there are going around saying that it never happened. It’s being erased in almost Orwellian fashion. And that, as a jazz historian, pisses me off you know I mean whenever I get a chance to correct that I’m very vocal about that because I think it’s important that people get recognition for what they’ve done, which, and for example I’m glad that you’ve been doing all these interviews for 25, 30 years. I mean you’ve interviewed a lot of people who otherwise would not have gotten that recognition or gotten the chance to tell their stories. And it’s important that gets done.
